summary:
The Marshall Islands has no criminalisation regime covering same-sex conduct. Human Dignity Trust's global record of criminalisation history dates the country's decriminalisation to 2005, in the same period as repeals recorded for the United States in 2003 and for Cape Verde and San Marino in 2004. A visitor therefore faces no statutory offence for consensual same-sex relations.

No procedure for legal gender recognition is documented for the Marshall Islands. A traveller whose passport carries a gender marker changed in another country has no local route to amend documentation, and the marker on the document presented at entry is what border and screening officials will work from.

The most recent official country reporting in the inventory is the 2015 United States State Department Human Rights Report for the Marshall Islands. It identifies prison conditions, corruption and domestic violence as the significant problems under review, records no reports of torture, arbitrary killing or enforced disappearance, and reports no LGBT-specific abuses.

The Pacific Sexual and Gender Diversity Network profiles Anfernee Nenol Kaminaga, a 25-year-old pansexual genderqueer Marshallese who co-created and led Brighten the Rainbow, described as the first openly LGBTIQ initiative in the Marshall Islands. Openly LGBTIQ organising at that level exists, which bears on how visible a visitor's own presentation is likely to be received.

The population is very small and the evidence base thin. The absence of documented anti-trans or LGBT-specific abuse in official reporting is an absence of records rather than a demonstration of protection, and this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.
tangentialFactors:
The 2005 repeal places the Marshall Islands in a group of jurisdictions that ended same-sex conduct offences in the early 2000s, alongside the United States (2003), Cape Verde (2004) and San Marino (2004). That timing indicates a settled decriminalisation position rather than a provision under active challenge.

Domestic violence is named as a significant problem in the same official reporting that records no LGBT-specific abuses. General violence against persons in intimate settings is documented locally even where identity-based violence is not, so risk for a visitor attaches to interpersonal settings rather than to an identified anti-trans pattern.

Prison conditions are flagged as a significant problem and corruption as an institutional one. Both bear on what happens after any arrest or dispute, including the reliability of official remedies, though the reporting does not link either to LGBT detainees.

No reports of torture, arbitrary killing or enforced disappearance appear in the 2015 official record, and no later official country report is present in the inventory, so the enforcement picture cannot be dated more precisely than 2015.
localsOnly:
Residents have no legal mechanism for gender recognition: no statute or administrative process for changing a gender marker on civil documents is recorded for the Marshall Islands.

Domestic violence is documented as a significant problem affecting residents, alongside prison conditions and corruption in public institutions.

Openly LGBTIQ organising exists domestically. Anfernee Nenol Kaminaga co-created and led Brighten the Rainbow, characterised as the first openly LGBTIQ initiative in the country, and has held roles as a UNESCO Youth Ambassador and as a youth representative at the first UN Youth Climate Action Summit.

Same-sex conduct has been legal since 2005, so consensual relationships between adults carry no criminal penalty for residents either.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry and visa requirements for the Marshall Islands, including any screening question touching on gender identity or sexuality, are not covered by the sources in this inventory and remain unresolved.

The statement that no legal gender recognition exists is carried in the record without a primary statutory or government source in the current inventory; it should be verified against Marshallese legislation before being relied on as a finding.

The inventory contains no material on hate-crime or anti-discrimination provisions, on recognition of same-sex partners or marriages, or on access to gender-affirming healthcare. Whether such provisions exist is unresolved rather than confirmed absent.

Official human-rights reporting stops at 2015. Conditions after that date, including any change in the treatment of trans visitors, are not sourced here.
